header:
Date: 2028-11-18
Time: 16:00 - 16:47 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Erin McAllister (NyxWorks CTO), Samir Gupta (Head of Platform), Rita Huang (Security PM), Leo Park (Backend Engineer), Jules (NyxWorks note-taker)
summary: Exploratory discovery focused on integrating Redwood for NyxWorks' LLM features. Discussion covered hosted vs dedicated vs private deployments, SDK adapters (Python/Node), LangChain and LlamaIndex integration patterns, gateway/proxy topology and where to surface rate limits/quotas, and observability hooks (token-level metrics, traces, and KV cache visibility). Customer is leaning toward a hybrid proof-of-concept: hosted for early rollout, dedicated/private for PII-sensitive flows. Action items and pilot plan agreed.
topics: Deployment modes: hosted vs dedicated vs private
SDK integration: Python/Node and server-side SDKs
LangChain & LlamaIndex adapters and prompt templating
Gateway/proxy patterns and sidecar vs centralized gateway
Rate limiting and quota enforcement details
Observability: token-level metrics, tracing, dashboards, audit logs
Security controls: SSO/SAML, KMS, SOC2, data residency
transcript: 00:00 Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — this is Maya from Redwood, AE on the account. Diego is our SE. How's everyone doing?
00:06 Erin: Good, thanks. Busy week but excited to dig in. We wanted to talk through how Redwood would fit into our stack, esp with our edge proxy setup.

00:14 Diego: Great — quick intro from us, we typically help customers pick between hosted, dedicated and private and then align integration patterns with their gateway and LLM orchestration. We'll ask about traffic, SLAs, security, etc.

00:30 Samir: Quick context: NyxWorks runs a global microservice mesh, edge proxies in front of region clusters. We have a central API gateway but also run sidecars for latency-sensitive paths. Typical 95th p99 latency goals for user-facing LLM features are around 250ms. We do about 120 requests/sec during peaks, avg token lengths moderate, and spikes in mornings.

00:52 Maya: Thanks — that helps. Two immediate questions: 1) Do you expect PII/data residency constraints that would push you to private/dedicated right away? 2) How tightly coupled do you want the inference runtime to be to your gateway?

01:08 Erin: For initial pilot, we can use hosted for non-PII. But for our support product we may need a private deployment or VPC. We'll need audit logs and KMS integration for secrets on the private flows.
01:22 Rita: Security side — we'll need SOC2, SSO/SAML for console access, and the ability to push audit logs to our SIEM. Also encryption at rest with customer-managed keys ideally.

01:33 Diego: Understood. We have SOC2 and options for KMS/HSM integrations on Private, and for Dedicated we can support customer-owned VPC peering. Audit log export to Seq/Datadog/Splunk is common — we can push structured logs. I'll upload the security pack after this call.
01:52 Leo: On integration — we use LangChain in the app layer and sometimes LlamaIndex for retrieval augmented generation. How do your SDKs play with these? Any adapter code to avoid reinventing?
02:03 Maya: Yes, great question. Diego: can you speak to the LangChain/LlamaIndex connectors?

02:08 Diego: Sure — we provide Python and Node SDKs that behave like a drop-in transport. For LangChain we have an examples repo with a RedwoodLLM wrapper that implements the chain interface; for LlamaIndex we show how to use embeddings and store vectors, plus config for streaming and chunking. We'll share the repo link. The adapter handles tokenization differences and streaming callbacks.
02:37 Erin: How does streaming work if we route through our own gateway? We're worried about timeouts and partial responses being dropped by proxies.

02:47 Diego: Two approaches: 1) Keep a direct connection from client to Redwood streaming endpoint (less hops) or 2) proxy with websockets or chunked responses through your gateway. If you have sidecars, the sidecar can maintain the connection and stream to client. We recommend configuring long-lived connections at the gateway and increasing proxy read timeouts for streamed endpoints. There's a sample nginx config in our docs.
03:12 Samir: For us, sidecar streaming seems cleaner since we already have that pattern. We'll need examples for nginx and envoy timeouts though. Also how does prefix/KV cache work across restarts?

03:25 Diego: KV cache is per-inference process by default; for Dedicated/Private you can configure persistent KV cache backed by Redis to survive restarts. For hosted customers we handle caching in the runtime and can expose metrics like cache hit rates. We'll show you cache metrics and suggestions to tune TTLs.
03:44 Erin: Rate limits — we want per-route quotas and per-tenant quotas. Where should enforcement live? Upstream gateway or Redwood?

03:52 Maya: Great point — both options valid. If you enforce at the gateway you save on tokens/calls to Redwood but you need to mirror billing quotas. Redwood supports token-level rate limits and per-key quotas, and you can also propagate headers from your gateway for tenant identification. Many customers do a hybrid: gateway blocks obviously malicious floods, Redwood enforces billing and fine-grained quota per API key.
04:18 Samir: If we push enforcement to our gateway, how do we get accurate token counts for billing? We want to reconcile usage for internal chargeback.

04:27 Diego: We expose per-request token metadata in response headers and through our usage API. You can pull aggregated token usage from the API and import into your billing systems. If gateway blocks a request before it hits Redwood, it won't be billed — so we recommend emitting a consistent token-estimate header from gateway using your tokenizer libs so internal accounting matches post-factum billing from Redwood.
04:55 Rita: About observability — we need traces end-to-end, and token-level cost breakdown per route. Does Redwood provide tracing spans usable with OpenTelemetry?

05:04 Diego: Yes, we emit spans and can integrate with OpenTelemetry. For tracing we include span context tags for model, sequence length, KV cache hits, and batching latencies. Token-level cost is available per request in the telemetry payload and ingestible by your metrics backend. There's also a per-route dashboard in Redwood Console that maps tokens, latency P95/99, and errors.
05:28 Erin: Excellent. Can the console export dashboards or webhook alerts for regressions? We want to alert on model output quality drop and latency spikes.

05:36 Maya: You can set monitors and alerts with webhook sinks; we also support regressions tied to eval sets so you can get notified when a prompt set drops below a threshold. Diego, maybe mention eval hooks?

05:45 Diego: Right — Redwood Optimize can run periodic evals against pinned prompts and send alerts if accuracy or hallucination metrics change. Integration is via an API to push prompt sets and reference outputs. Many customers wire this into their CI to gate rollouts.
06:02 Leo: On rollout strategy — we want canary and automatic fallback if latency SLOs are missed. Can Redwood do model variant fallback?

06:09 Diego: Yes. Smart routing can fallback to a lower-cost variant or a region-specific replica if latency or capacity thresholds are hit. For Dedicated you can configure reserved capacity and fallback routes to hosted for overflow. We can demo routing rules in the console.
06:28 Samir: Latency SLOs: p99 under 250ms. Can we get benchmarks for your runtime with our token lengths?

06:35 Maya: We should schedule a benchmarking session. For that we'll need a representative prompt set and traffic profile. Diego can run microbenchmarks and we can run an end-to-end pilot using our dedicated pool or hosted endpoints, depending on what you want to validate.

06:51 Erin: Pilot scope question — we'd like to test: 1) LangChain integration + streaming, 2) Observability hooks into Datadog, 3) Rate-limits mapping, and 4) Private deploy feasibility for PII path. Is that reasonable for a 4-week pilot?

07:05 Maya: Yes, that's a realistic pilot. Typically week 1 onboarding and security review, week 2 SDK + adapter integration, week 3 run benchmarks and iterate, week 4 evaluate and decide on Dedicated vs Private. We'll capture that in the next steps.
07:18 Rita: Security gating — we'll require a pen test coordination and remote attestation for Private installs. Also a question: where are customer logs stored and how long are they retained?

07:28 Diego: For Hosted, logs are retained per your plan and can be exported; retention is configurable and you can opt for zero retention for sensitive flows. For Dedicated/Private you control retention and can forward logs to your SIEM. We'll include log retention examples in the security pack.
07:45 Jules (NyxWorks): note — Erin asked about zero retention option for specific tenants, flagged for action item.
07:51 Maya: Noted. Diego: quick demo idea — show LangChain snippet and proxy config?

07:56 Diego: Yeah I'll share a short example now verbally and then upload the code. Basic flow: install redwood-sdk, instantiate Redwood client with streaming callback, wrap in a LangChain LLM wrapper implementing generate/stream methods, and configure LlamaIndex data connector to call the embeddings endpoint. For gateways, we include an envoy filter example to forward chunked responses and preserve streaming semantics.
08:22 Leo: Does the SDK implement token counting or do we need a separate tokenizer to estimate tokens before gateway enforcement?

08:30 Diego: SDK returns token usage after the call, but we also have a lightweight tokenizer in the SDK for pre-call estimates. Many customers embed that at the gateway for quota enforcement approximations.
08:45 Erin: On pricing — we need an estimate for the pilot (approx 100k tokens/day). Also pricing differences hosted vs dedicated contracts?

08:54 Maya: We'll send a pilot quote. Hosted has pay-as-you-go pricing, Dedicated is a reserved capacity model with a monthly commit and lower per-token rate. Private adds platform fee and some professional services for on-prem. I'll attach the pricing sheet to the follow-up email.
09:08 Samir: One more thing: our observability team wants to correlate user request IDs across our gateway, the Redwood request, and downstream vector DB calls. How best to pass trace ids?

09:18 Diego: Pass the trace/span context headers; we honor W3C tracecontext headers and add them into our spans. We'll include an example where you forward x-request-id and traceparent headers through the proxy and Redwood surfaces them in the logs and traces so you can join across systems.
09:35 Rita: Are there RBAC controls for who can deploy new model versions via the console? We want separation of duties.
09:41 Maya: Yes, RBAC with SSO/SAML, role definitions, and audit trails for rollout operations. For Dedicated/Private you can enforce restrictions via your identity provider.
09:52 Erin: Curious about quantization/accelerators — if we go Dedicated, can you recommend optimized model variants or quantized versions to hit cost targets?

09:59 Diego: Absolutely — part of Redwood Optimize we provide quantization and kernel-selection recommendations based on your sequence length distributions. We can recommend INT8 or mixed-precision variants and show estimated cost savings and latency tradeoffs.

10:14 Samir: On the proxy topology: we're evaluating two patterns — a centralized gateway that forwards to Redwood and a per-service sidecar that handles retries/streaming. Which do you see customers picking?

10:25 Diego: Both exist. Sidecars reduce hop count and are easier for streaming. Centralized gateways simplify policy enforcement (auth, quotas). If you need strong tenant isolation and token-level billing accuracy, sidecar + internal auth header propagation is a good compromise. We'll provide both patterns in the integration doc.
10:45 Leo: For quotas, if we do per-tenant keys, are there tooling APIs for changing quotas dynamically?
10:51 Maya: Yes, quota APIs and admin endpoints allow programmatic updates. We also expose usage webhooks so you can auto-scale quotas based on internal signals.
11:02 Erin: Let's talk risk scenarios — what happens if Redwood has an incident, how do we fail gracefully?

11:07 Diego: We recommend defining fallback strategies: client-side degrade to cached answers, a cheaper hosted fallback model, or queueing. Redwood supports automated fallback to pinned variants and to regional replicas. For Dedicated contracts we have SLA and optional standby capacity.
11:22 Samir: SLA numbers? Uptime and latency guarantees for Dedicated?

11:26 Maya: Dedicated SLAs include 99.9% uptime and latency SLO targets based on instance types. We'll share the SLA doc. Private deployments can have a custom SLA as negotiated in the enterprise agreement.
11:40 Rita: Data residency — we need EU-only for some customers. Can you restrict hosting region?
11:45 Maya: Yes, you can pin workloads to regions. For Private you operate in your DC. For Hosted we offer region selection for endpoints so data doesn't leave region.
11:58 Jules: note — region pinning and EU-only requirement captured as constraint.

12:03 Diego: A small technical caveat: if you do cross-region fallbacks, you'll want to consider latency and compliance implications. For leaked PII you should use Private or Dedicated with strict routing policies.
12:18 Erin: Ok — on the POC can you show an example where we send a prompt through our gateway, Redwood streams the response, and Datadog receives traces/metrics?

12:27 Diego: Yes — that's the baseline POC. We'll prepare a step-by-step runbook: 1) Create sandbox API key, 2) Hook SDK in a LangChain test app, 3) Configure gateway timeouts and streaming proxy, 4) Enable Datadog exporter in Redwood Console, 5) Run load with your traffic profile. We'll demo trace maps and token cost charts.
12:52 Samir: About authentication between our gateway and Redwood — prefer mTLS or API keys?

12:58 Maya: API keys are simplest for Hosted. For Dedicated/Private, mutual TLS is supported and often used for stronger identity. We also support short-lived creds via token exchange if you want ephemeral keys.
13:12 Leo: Any gotchas with LlamaIndex when using managed embeddings? We use local vector DB but need embedding consistency.

13:19 Diego: Ensure you pin embedding model version and replicate normalization steps. We include an example showing how to store embedding metadata and hashing to detect drift. Also we surface embedding logs to help debug mismatch.
13:36 Erin: One more product question — do you support function/tool-calling or structured outputs?
13:41 Diego: Yes, Redwood supports function calling and structured output with enforced schema validation. That can be integrated into LangChain flows too.
13:50 Samir: Great. Any references or docs we should read now?
13:55 Maya: I'll drop links: SDK quickstart, LangChain adapter repo, security pack, and a sample benchmarking plan. Also the price sheet.
14:03 Rita: On pen test coordination — who do we contact?
14:06 Maya: I'll include the security contact in the follow-up email and cc Diego for technical coordination.
14:12 Jules: note — pen test contact to be added.
14:17 Diego: Quick question for you Samir — can you send over token distribution and a representative prompt set after the call? That will make benchmarks realistic.
14:25 Samir: Yep, we'll share that. Expect to send a sample by 2028-11-22.

14:30 Maya: Great — so recapping: we'll send security pack and SOC2, Diego will share LangChain/LlamaIndex example repo and proxy configs, we'll propose pilot pricing and infra diagram, Samir will share traffic/prompt data, and we'll schedule a benchmarking session week of 2028-11-29. Anything else?
14:47 Erin: Nope that's it from us. Thanks Maya/Diego — this was helpful.
14:52 Maya: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the artifacts. Bye.
14:55 Diego: Thanks, bye.
